title: Mobility remains car-dependent and safety-constrained even as people support shared, active and lower-carbon alternatives
geography: 31 countries and markets; global, regional and country comparisons

denominator.unit: adults surveyed across 31 countries and markets; country age frames vary

car_free_impossibility.unit: percent saying living without a car would be impossible

car_preference.unit: percent saying the car is the transport mode they enjoy most

car_preference_country_count.unit: countries out of 31 where the car is the most preferred transport mode

walking_enjoyment.unit: percent saying walking is the transport mode they enjoy most

observations.method: Ipsos Global Advisor survey of mobility choices, enjoyment and perceived necessity across 31 countries and markets.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported car dependence reflects built environment, work and care geography, income, disability, safety and preference; it is not a trip diary or causal estimate of infrastructure constraint.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 31 countries and markets, with country and regional variation.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may describe car ownership as impossible because it is convenient or socially expected rather than because no viable alternative exists.

observations.period: 2026; perceived access, affordability and safety of public transport

denominator.unit: countries and markets in the Ipsos Mobility Report

public_transport_accessible.unit: average percent viewing public transport as accessible

public_transport_safe.unit: average percent viewing public transport as safe

rural_access_affordability_boundary.value: Affordability and access lag in rural areas

public_transport_and_care.value: Mobility determines who can reach jobs, schools and care

observations.method: Cross-national public-attitude comparison of transport access, safety and affordability, interpreted in relation to inclusion and daily destinations.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived access and safety do not establish service frequency, reliability, travel time, fare burden or actual ability to reach essential destinations.
observations.subgroup: Residents across 31 countries and markets, with rural/urban and age differences noted in the report.
observations.counterinterpretation: A transport mode can be perceived as accessible and safe while remaining unusable for people with irregular schedules, disabilities, care burdens or long-distance commutes.

denominator.unit: countries and markets in the Ipsos Mobility Report

road_safety_concern.unit: percent worried about road safety in their area

residential_speed_limit_support.unit: percent supporting lower speed limits in residential areas

motorway_speed_limit_support.unit: percent supporting lower speed limits on motorways or freeways

g7_motorway_support.unit: percent support for lower motorway speed limits among G7 countries

observations.method: Cross-national survey of perceived road danger and support for traffic-law and speed-limit interventions.
observations.uncertainty: Support for rules is an attitude measure; it does not estimate compliance, enforcement, travel-time trade-offs or crash reduction.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 31 countries and markets, with comparisons across residential and motorway settings and the G7.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may support safety interventions where they see direct local risk while resisting changes that threaten speed, freight or long-distance mobility.

denominator.unit: countries and markets in the Ipsos Mobility Report

self_driving_safe.unit: percent who would feel safe riding in a self-driving car

self_driving_unsafe.unit: percent who would feel unsafe riding in a self-driving car

dedicated_cycle_lane_support.unit: percent supporting dedicated cycle lanes on roads

cycle_lane_opposition.unit: percent opposed to dedicated cycle lanes

ev_appeal.unit: percent finding driving an electric vehicle appealing

ev_adoption_expectation.unit: percent expecting many consumers to adopt EVs by 2030

observations.method: Cross-national comparison of trust in autonomous vehicles, support for active-mobility infrastructure and expectations about EV adoption.
observations.uncertainty: Stated safety and appeal do not predict purchase, use or local consent; autonomous-vehicle and EV views depend on infrastructure, price, privacy, reliability and policy context.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 31 countries and markets; Ipsos reports higher self-driving confidence in Asia-Pacific and Latin America and greater unease in Europe and North America.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public support for cycle lanes and EVs can coexist with continued car dependence because people may support alternatives without having a feasible substitute for daily travel.

related_sources.claim: Official Ipsos April 2026 publication PDF containing the Mobility Report summary and headline figures.
Official Ipsos country-language report page with additional autonomy, car-dependence and road-safety comparisons.

boundary: This record adds a mobility-dependency mechanism: people remain attached to cars because access, time and daily destinations are structured around them, while broad support exists for safer streets, cycle lanes, public transport and lower-carbon vehicles. It is a cross-national public-attitude survey, not a travel diary, service-quality audit, crash dataset, engineering assessment or proof that stated support produces modal shift.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ipsos Mobility Report page, April 2026 publication PDF and French report page were retrieved and reviewed for car dependence, mode enjoyment, public-transport access and safety, rural boundary, road-safety concern, speed-limit support, autonomous-vehicle trust, cycle-lane support and EV expectations; the official summary PDF was hashed.
